## ABSTRACT

In this article I present the findings of my ethnographic research with local cryptocurrency activists in London and Geneva. Local cryptocurrencies circulate within a specific delimited geographic area, often a city or district, ensuring spatial proximity between users. Using Giacomo Bazzani's categories of feasible, near-future expectations and uncertain and usually distant imaginaries, I explore the future visions of these activists through the lens of the anthropology and sociology of the future. Their expectations include decentralized funding and the ability to provide trusted, secure payments, for which they have chosen blockchain as an ally. Their imaginaries are based on a societal shift to post-individual or modern Gemeinschaft communities practicing direct democracy and cooperative local trade. This research contributes to the theoretical understanding of imagination and how social movements navigate between pragmatic expectations and radical imaginaries, revealing the inherent tensions in balancing feasibility with transformative potential. The study also illuminates the shifting architecture of trust in alternative economic systems, from reliance on state institutions and community trust to faith in algorithmic authority and perceived mathematical certainty. All the future visions I encountered during my fieldwork fall under the category of left-leaning blockchain commons, challenging dominant narratives within the cryptocurrency ecosystem.

## In the minds of future-makers

Following the call by Arjun Appadurai in his seminal The Future as Cultural Fact (Citation 2013), I examine narratives that envision an imaginary future and thereby shed light on the desires, challenges, and needs of the present, as well as the aspirations, hopes, and fears. Rather than taking a traditional anthropological focus on past and present societies, I explore the hoped-for futures in the minds of those who organize alternative payment schemes. During my fieldwork, I attempt to comprehend how local cryptocurrency (LCC) promoters anticipate and conceive both the future and their role in its construction. In this article I present the short and long-term visions imagined by LCC activists in London and Geneva who have developed, respectively, the Brixton Pound (BP) and the Monnaie Léman (ML). Both currencies existed in non-crypto form as local currencies (LCs), but they later decided to employ blockchain technology. Thus, my research captures the moment when LCs are becoming local cryptocurrencies (LCCs) and explores the reasons behind this transition. Using Giacomo Bazzani’s (Citation 2023) categories of feasible, near-future expectations and uncertain and usually distant imaginaries, I discuss BP and ML visions through the lens of the anthropology and sociology of the future. These categories can apply to both individual and societal levels. My findings provide a unique insight into the marketplace of ideas, in which the expectations and imaginaries arising from these social movements compete and add value. Technology – blockchain and cryptocurrency in these cases – often serves as a promise, hope, and accelerator of a better future, ‘a shortcut towards alternative futures’ (Keere and Novokreshchenov Citation 2024, 3). Thus, I also address why social movements that experiment with money have chosen blockchain as an ally and the narratives that position this technology as advantageous. Taking an interdisciplinary approach encompassing anthropology, sociology, and, to a lesser extent, economics, I will first clarify the rationale, validity, and relevance of the categories I utilize, and describe how I have collected my data. I then explain the basic features of blockchain, attitudes towards this technology within the LCC movement, and the ways it has been utilized by these partly anarcho-communist activists. In order to explore the expectations and imaginaries conceived by these activists, I introduce the idea of left-leaning blockchain commons. These expectations include decentralized funding (BP), and trusted, secure payment (ML, BP). The imaginaries include direct democracy (BP) and the potential for new types of communities. Although termed post-individual Footnote 1 in Brixton and modern Gemeinschaft Footnote 2 in Geneva (ML), as I will discuss, these envisioned future communities have significant similarities.

### Category definitions and a rationale for studying the future

The social movements that I have studied are driven by their imaginaries of the future, which motivate them to strive for social change. Based on the work of radical imagination, imaginaries, whether of hopeful or fearsome futures, are characterized by an open future far from the realities of the present and usually long-term temporalities (Bazzani Citation 2023). They are therefore distinct from the short-term temporalities of expectations, the near-future deliberations and immediate plans of which engender practical consciousness and actions anchored in existing institutions and social structures (Bazzani Citation 2023). To Bazzani's discussion, I add the notion that imagination can be equally attributed to both expectations and imaginaries, rather than solely to imaginaries, as the original theory suggests (Bazzani Citation 2023, 388). I distinguish two types of expectations – conventional and imaginative. C onventional expectations are associated with actions based on established routines, business-as-usual approaches, and mechanical operations. In contrast, while rooted in practical considerations and the constraints of existing structures, imaginative expectations leverage the power of imagination to propose innovative approaches that push the boundaries of the current paradigm, always remaining mindful of real-world feasibility, echoing John Holloway's concept of crack capitalism: 

How do we change the world? (…) There is no Right Answer, just millions of experiments. (…) There is never any purity in these experiments, thank goodness. All are contradictory. (…) The indigenous organisation that accepts funds from a church dedicated to subordination and misogyny, the radical professor who participates in the quantitative measurement of student's work, the cooperative that sells its products on the market, the car worker who spends most of his time producing objects that kill and contaminate and then organize a community garden in the evenings and at weekends (…). We try to overcome contradictions, we rebel against our own complicity, we try in every way to stop making capitalism. (…) We are part of the social flow of rebellion, and in this flow there is no room for rigidities and hard lines. The concept of correctness and betrayal, its complement that is so rooted in the culture of the left, are obstacles to the flow of rebellion. (Citation 2010, 257–258)

I define imaginative expectations as action strategies that lay the groundwork for achieving possible imaginaries. Imaginaries, in turn, may become achievable in the distant future, but only if certain imaginative expectations have paved the way for their realization. However, imaginaries may also remain unattainable, inherently uncertain, and difficult to assess in terms of feasibility when projected far into the future. Conversely, imaginaries may be short-term if these immediate visions are highly divorced from feasibility, disconnected from the present context and expected dynamics, and thus contribute to a ‘departure from the space of experience’ (Bazzani Citation 2023, 387). In the case of the local cryptocurrencies discussed in this article, their initiatives can be categorized as imaginative expectations and imaginaries. From now on, I will use expectations as shorthand, with the implicit understanding that I mean imaginative expectations.

Not every social movement is guided by imaginaries; some merely respond to current issues. The LCC activists I conducted fieldwork with engage in the social endeavor of building compelling stories of the immediate and distant future, an undertaking that exhibits a performative effect. Competing in the marketplace of ideas for the future, they form what Nancy Fraser (Citation 1990) has termed subaltern counterpublics to challenge dominant narratives within the public sphere. Aware of the force of stories of the future, technological companies commodify these by giving clients a sense of mastering the unfamiliar. For example, the way in which Facebook promotes its tools presents the company as a social movement rather than a profit-making machine (Haupt Citation 2021). With stories of the future playing a role as potent marketing devices (Mager and Katzenbach Citation 2021), convincing future narratives can determine the strength of a social movement. The initiatives I have studied are guided by the principle outlined by Gümüsay and Reinecke (Citation 2022, 241): ‘If we don't imagine the future, others like technology companies will’.

Mager and Katzenbach (Citation 2021, 1) have argued that ‘visions of the future are omnipresent in current debates about digital transformation’. While digital acceleration can provide hope, it also deepens cultural instability and amplifies fears. Thus, visions of technological utopias and, more commonly, dystopias, provide orientation and mitigate uncertainty (Beckert Citation 2019). Future narratives help us understand technological features and their possible and impossible uses in various social settlements and assemblages of human and non-human actors. Serving as vitally important cognitive tools, they can prompt social action to achieve a desired future or suspend actions that are deemed detrimental.

However, the pivotal issues remain the quality of these imaginative expectations and imaginaries and which, produced by whom, are the most compelling. Jens Beckert argues that the exhaustion of neoliberalism's futures has not led to a rebirth of alternative imagination but rather to its anomie, creating a situation where the gap in narrating a promissory future remains unfilled, resulting in a profound social crisis (Beckert Citation 2019, 10). Paradoxically, despite its exhaustion, neoliberalism persists as an unconquered zombie ideology (Fisher Citation 2008, 15). Beckert asserts that mobilizing society and implementing change is impossible without a compelling vision of the future (termed promissory legitimacy). Yet, Beckert emphasizes that imagination alone is likely insufficient: 

That such an imaginary has not yet emerged might not owe simply to a lack of imagination. It might also be that the entrenchment of current economic and political structures forecloses the possibility of change along such lines and thus precludes realistic hope for such an alternative.
